title: Inspiring Leaders and Reliable Ones
text:
For decades, leadership researchers had distinguished two broad kinds of leaders. Transformational leaders inspire people with a vision, set an example, challenge them intellectually and attend to their individual growth. Transactional leaders run on clear exchanges: they set expectations and reward people when the work is done, or they watch for mistakes and correct them. A third pattern, laissez-faire leadership, means avoiding decisions and being absent when needed.

In 2004 Timothy Judge and Ronald Piccolo combined the results of 87 earlier studies to see how each kind of leadership related to outcomes such as follower satisfaction, motivation, leader effectiveness and group performance.

Transformational leadership had the strongest overall link with good outcomes. But contingent reward, the core of transactional leadership, was nearly as strongly related, and in some settings it was even stronger. The two styles were also closely correlated: good leaders tended to do both. Laissez-faire leadership, by contrast, was clearly linked to worse results, nearly as harmful as transformational leadership was helpful.
lesson: Inspiring people matters, but so does reliably keeping your word on goals and rewards. What damages a team most is a leader who is simply absent.
source: Judge, T. A., and Piccolo, R. F. (2004). Transformational and transactional leadership: A meta-analytic test of their relative validity. Journal of Applied Psychology, 89(5), 755-768.
caveat: Much of the underlying data came from questionnaires answered by followers, which may blur the line between liking a leader and judging their results.
